cultivar: Fengqing large-leaf and other Yunnan big-leaf (assamica) cultivars such as Yunkang 10
processing: Fully oxidised: a bud with one or two leaves is withered, rolled, oxidised for a few hours in warm humid rooms and dried with hot air; the thick golden down on Yunnan buds stays gold through oxidation.
harvest_season: Spring (March–April) is the main and best harvest; autumn lots are fragrant and cheaper, summer lots are the plain ones.
appearance_dry: Fat, twisted dark-brown to black leaves threaded with golden tips, more tips the higher the grade.
appearance_liquor: Bright red-orange, clear, with a golden ring at the edge of the cup.
appearance_wet: Large, soft copper-red leaves and buds, very even in colour.
taste_profile: Malt and honey with a baked sweet-potato note, cocoa and a peppery brightness in the middle steeps, finishing soft and sugary with gentle grip.

brewing.notes: Forgiving tea: 90–95 °C keeps the sweetness ahead of the tannin, boiling water will not wreck it. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes, takes milk well.

vintage_note: Sold by the current year's harvest, usually spring (March–April) with autumn lots as a cheaper second choice. It is at its best within a year of picking, though decent Dian Hong stays pleasant for two or three years in a sealed bag. Sun-dried shai hong is the only Yunnan black sold by vintage and aged on purpose.
description:
Dian Hong is Yunnan's black tea, and the classic gongfu style is the one with twisted dark leaves threaded with golden tips. It is a young tea by Chinese standards: it was developed in 1938–39 in Shunning, today's Fengqing County in Lincang, when black-tea makers were sent to Yunnan to turn the province's big-leaf trees into an export black during the war. The big-leaf assamica plant is what makes it different from Keemun or a Fujian gongfu: more body, more malt, and a sweetness that tastes of baked sweet potato.

The leaf – a bud with one or two leaves from Fengqing large-leaf bushes and related Yunnan cultivars – is withered, rolled, oxidised in warm humid rooms and dried with hot air. Yunnan buds carry thick golden down that stays gold through oxidation, so the proportion of tips is both a grade marker and a sign of how early the picking was.

Brewed gongfu it starts malty and honeyed with that sweet-potato note, picks up cocoa and a peppery brightness in the middle steeps, and fades to a soft, sugary finish. It is forgiving: boiling water will not wreck it the way it does a delicate Fujian black, though 90–95 °C keeps the sweetness ahead of the tannin. Western-style, 3 g per 250 ml for three minutes makes a rich cup that takes milk well.

Fengqing is the heart of production, but Lincang generally, Baoshan, Pu'er, Dehong and Xishuangbanna all make Dian Hong, and a good label names the county. Grades run from Te Ji (special) downward, with 'Jin Hao' (golden tip) lots above them; broken CTC Dian Hong for export is a different, cheaper product. Buy the current spring harvest; autumn lots are fragrant and cheaper, summer lots are the plain ones.

If you want to climb the ladder, the all-bud Golden Buds (Jin Ya) and Golden Needle are the sweet, pricy end; old-tree (gu shu) Dian Hong is the complex end.
